title: Part 4: Is the University Discriminatory?
text:
In this post, we explore how gender can influence pay in universities - even when men and women have similar experience, degrees, and responsibilities.
We looked at faculty salaries at a large university from 1976 to 1995. To get a clear “snapshot” of the situation, we focused on the most recent year, 1995. This way, we could see the accumulated effects of pay practices over time.
To make a fair comparison, we considered factors like:
Essentially, we asked: “If men and women had the same qualifications, would they earn the same?”

title: Part 4: Is the University Discriminatory?
text:
How We Measured Fair Pay?
We built two simple “prediction models” for salaries:

Fair Model: Predicts salary based on qualifications and responsibilities alone.
Full Model: Adds gender to see if it explains any extra differences in pay.

If adding gender improves the prediction, it suggests there’s a gender-based pay gap that isn’t explained by experience, rank, or field.

title: Part 4: Is the University Discriminatory?
text:
What We Found?
Our analysis revealed a clear pattern:
In 1995, men earned about $298 more per month than women with the same qualifications and duties. This difference is statistically significant, which means it’s unlikely to be due to random chance.
We also looked at how rank affects the gap through predictions models:

When controlling for rank, the pay gap is smaller ($298/month), reflecting unequal pay within the same rank.
When ignoring rank, the gap grows to $420/month, highlighting a “glass ceiling” effect where women are less likely to hold higher-paying senior positions.

We analysed the Rank distribution among both genders and found men are heavily represented in the highest faculty ranks, while women are more concentrated in lower ranks. This explains part of the total pay gap.
Female faculty face a double disadvantage:

They are paid less than men within the same rank.
They are underrepresented in senior positions, which offer higher salaries.

Combined, these effects can add up to significant financial inequality over a career. Even when men and women have the same experience, qualifications, and responsibilities, systematic pay gaps exist.

title: Part 2: Is There Bias from Day One?
text:
After reviewing the introduction and gaining a brief understanding of the data we are working with in this analysis, consider this question to yourself;
“Does wage discrimination actually exist in the starting salaries between men and women faculty members?” 
What is the instinctive answer that comes to your mind?
Well, to determine if a bias actually exists in the starting salaries, we will first have to adjust our data from our original dataset, with almost 20,000 entries, to a dataset which only looks at salary in a professor’s starting year. What we noticed was that since the original data was recorded from 1976 to 1995, not all faculty members had a recorded starting salary. So we went from the original 1,597 faculty to only 1,107!
We then used two simple methods to test for the difference in between the starting salary of men and women, one testing for a difference in the average starting salary of the two groups and another testing for whether gender had an effect on salary when other variables are taken into consideration. 
We first calculated the average starting salary of men to be $4015.55 and the average starting salary for women to be $3600.32, which displays an obvious difference of $415.23. We then used statistical analysis to determine if this was a significant difference and we found that it was! 
This suggests that assuming salary is only affected by gender, male faculty members on average make $415.23 more than women faculty members!
Now you may be an astute reader and have noticed the super important phrasing of “assuming salary is only affected by gender”. Do you think gender still has an effect on salary when other predictor variables are included?
We conducted a second approach to verify the effect of gender on salary by testing a base model (where “sex” is not included) and a full model (where “sex” is included) to see if there is a significant effect of gender on salary when other aspects such as the starting year, field, rank etc. are incorporated into the model. It turns out that after controlling for all other predictor variables, sex still explains a significant amount of variation in salary.
From our analysis, we found that starting year, field, admin, and rank also had significant effects on starting salaries. When we take these four variables into account, the effect of gender on starting salary also changed as described below. When all other variables are held constant:

Male faculty members’ starting salary is 5.46% higher than their female counterparts.
Professors in the field categorized as “Other” have a starting salary that is 10.89% higher than those in the “Arts”.
Professors in the Professional field have a starting salary that is 24.99% higher than those in the “Arts”.
Faculty members with administration experience have a starting salary that is 13.57% higher than faculty members without administration experience.
Faculty members ranked as “Associate” have a starting salary that is 26.17% higher than faculty members ranked as “Assistant”.
Faculty members ranked as “Full” have a starting salary that is 79.49% higher than faculty members ranked as Assistant.


When looking at the starting year, starting salary increases by 5.77% per year, which is a potential indication for inflation. 
So to answer the question in short, Yes! wage discrimination does exist in the starting salaries of men and women faculty members!  This is reflected in both the average starting salary and the effect of gender on salary when other variables are incorporated. Although starting salary is also affected by categories such as rank, field, and admin, and even more affected by the starting year, the test conducted in this analysis provides significant evidence of a difference between the starting salaries of women and men faculty members in general.

title: Part 7: Wrapping Up
text:
While we spent the last two posts discussing issues with the analysis methods and the data collection itself, we still found interesting findings! What did we truly learn about gender equity at this institution?

We found a significant gap in starting salaries. Right from day one, women were at a disadvantage, earning less than their male colleagues even with similar backgrounds.
While we found no gender discrimination in promotion raises (in fact, women’s raises were slightly higher in some models!), these jumps were not large enough to close the initial gap created at the time of hire.
Because of that early “starting line” difference, the 1995 snapshot shows a persistent overall pay gap. Even when men and women reached the same level of experience and responsibility, the shadow of the starting salary followed them throughout their careers.

While our data and methods had some limitations, the message is clear: The university’s pay gap isn’t about how people are promoted; it’s about how they are hired. Systematic discrimination exists not because the rules change halfway through, but because they start unequally. To truly achieve equity, the university must focus on closing the gap at the point of entry. Thank you for reading our seven part series on gender discrimination at a university! We hope this analysis serves as a starting point for more transparent and fair conversations about faculty compensation.

title: Part 1: Are Salaries Fair?
text:
Have you ever wondered if men and women are truly paid the same for doing the same job? In the United States, we often hear that women earn less than men, even when they have the same experience and positions. But is this really happening inside our universities?
To find the truth, our team decided to go beyond the headlines and look at the actual numbers. We analyzed data from a major U.S. university involving 1,597 faculty members. We wanted to see if the “fairness” we expect in education is reflected in their paychecks.
Over the next few posts, we will answer four big questions:

The Starting Salary: Do men and women start with the same salary when they are first hired?
The Promotion Boost: When professors get promoted (from Associate to Full Professor), do they get the same pay raise?
The Big Picture: Overall, is there clear evidence of gender pay discrimination at this university?
The Reality Check: Can we apply these findings to other universities or to the world today?

But first, lets talk data.
Oue data itself includes nine variables.

case: acts as an index, so each row gets its own value
sex: is a binary variable. This means it can only take on two values: male or female
deg: is again binary and refers to the type of degree a professor has (either “Professional” or “PhD”
yrdeg: the year a professor achieved their degree
field: is the specific school a professor works in (“Arts”, “Professional”, or “Other”)
startyr: is the year a professor was hired at the university
salary: the monthly salary (in USD) for a faculty member in that year
rank: the level of a professor (“Assistant”, “Associate” and “Full”). With associate being the lowest in the academic hierarchy and full being the highest
admin: is our final binary variable and indicates whether a faculty member has held administrative duties

But before we can dig into these variables, we had to make sure we were working with clean ingredients. We looked at data from 1976 to 1995 (excluding the medical school) and did some careful cleaning.
Sometimes, data comes with “missing pieces” (what we call NA or empty spots). For example, a few records didn’t list a professor’s rank. Since we can’t analyze what we don’t know, we removed those few incomplete entries. Don’t worry, though—it was only a tiny fraction of our data (just four out of thousands!), so it doesn’t change the overall story.
What’s next? Numbers can tell a powerful story, but they can also be tricky. In our next post, we’re going back to the very beginning: The Day of Hiring.
Does the pay gap start on day one?
Stay tuned to find out!

title: Part 6: Trust the Data?
text:
The other way that our results may not be generalizable are things that occurred before we even started looking at the data. To start, we have no idea where this data was collected from! Different universities in the United States have very different starting salaries and that is due to the cost of living in certain areas. So looking at a University in downtown Seattle versus in rural Idaho, we would expect there to be very different salaries. We also may expect there to be differences culturally in what is allowed regarding sexist hiring policies. More conservative areas may have a higher rate of sexism in their workforce and may pay their women less.
The data also excludes medical school faculty, which makes sense since we may expect the starting salary for a medical school professor to be higher than the base salary for a non-medical school professor in general. However, this means that our findings are not easily applied to medical school faculty.
Throughout the analysis of our data our amazing researchers found multiple moments were we stopped and said “ugh I wish we had data for this”. For example, we wanted data on the race of each faculty member since race can often play a huge role in hiring. We are also missing key data that may be confounding the salaries such as age, publications, grants, teaching evaluations, and others that we may not have even thought of! Another issue is that data is collected from 1976 to 1995 and while we did normalize the salaries to be in 2026 dollars, sexism in the workplace has changed greatly from 1975 to 2026.
So as you can see, outside of the issues that arise with our modeling and analysis techniques–there are issues with the data itself!

title: Part 5: Trust in the Outcomes?
text:
In our next two posts we will discuss issues with generalizing what we have found so far! This is broken into two posts because there are two main areas where we can run into issues. The first is with our data analysis itself. Did we do things correctly? Did our models meet the necessary requirements? Lets find out!
All models have requirements of the data before you can run them! Some of those important requirements include that the data should be modeled using a line! Some graphs show curves or other shapes where a line would not be the right way to go! Thankfully our data did appear to work through a line model.
We also had to check that the data around the line that we modeled was equally random throughout! Even without a data science background if you look at a graph like this one: which shows the randomness around our line, we can see that the randomness is not the same distance from the line throughout! This is a problem in the data science world we call “lack of constant variance”. And since our data did not meet this requirement, we had to change our analysis approach to account for it!
So checking the data itself before we did any modeling helped us to avoid common errors that would affect our results negatively! This means that our modeling is a much better fit than if we had not checked these assumptions and are actually points in the positive for generalizing our results!

title: Part 3: Climbing the Ladder- The Promotion Gap
text:
In our last post, we looked at starting salaries. But now, what happens if a professor moves up the career ladder? Today, we are looking at one of the most important moments in a professor’s career: the promotion from Associate Professor to Full Professor.
When this promotion happens, it usually comes with a “salary jump” (a pay raise). So, we wanted to tackle a question: Do men get a bigger pay raise than women when they are promoted to Full professor?
First, we looked at over 500 professors who were promoted. Right away, we noticed a familiar pattern: the group was 82% men (446) and only 18% women (100).
When we looked at the average pay raise, the average jump was about $473 per month. Most people saw a nice increase, but one person actually saw their pay drop by $352. This could be attributed to the cessation of administrative stipends, grant-related funding adjustments, or potential data entry anomalies. For the purpose of this study, we retain these observations to maintain the integrity of the original dataset while acknowledging them as low-end outliers. On the other hand, one lucky person got a massive raise of over $2,805 monthly!

Then we looked at our charts, we saw something interesting. If you just look at the highest raises, a few men got much higher “jumps” than any of the women. In statistics, we call this “outliers” - people who don’t follow the normal pattern.
Because these few men got such huge raises, it can make it look like men are doing better overall. But is that actually true for the “average” professor?
To find the truth, we didn’t just look at gender. We also looked at:

What field do they work in? (e.g., Professional vs Arts)
When did they get their degree? (Seniority)
Do they have extra boss duties? (Administrative roles)

Here is what we found: When we compared a man and a woman in the same field, with the same experience, there was no evidence that men got more money. In fact, after we took out those few super high raises, we found that women actually got a slightly larger boost (about $60 more) than men!
So, it turns out that your gender isn’t what decides your promotion raise. The real factors are:

Your field: Professors in “Professional” fields (like Engineering) get much bigger raises than those in the Arts.
Timing: People who got their degrees more recently tend to see bigger jumps, likely because of inflation and newer university rules.

So, is there wage discrimination when getting promoted to “Full Professor”?
The answer is: No. While men still dominate the top ranks in terms of numbers, the actual pay raise given at the moment of promotion is fair. The differences we see in the data are mostly because of the specific job field or a few extreme cases, rather than a person’s gender. Coming up next: We’ll put all the pieces together to answer the big question: Is the university fair overall?
